finding: S1 and property 8 — the release gate — cannot both be satisfied, and the conflict is on S1's first four words rather than on the 'throughout it' half this round added. S1: 'The suite neither reads nor writes the repository's live review state.' Property 8 requires property 7 to hold 'for every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for', and §6.1 itself states that such an invocation writes: 'The tests invoke tp review and tp audit many times and both write the round snapshot (§2.2), so a suite run against the live tree would advance rounds it does not own while reporting green.' So the gate's own subject set is the live tree. The two doors §6.1 names are both shut for this property: --no-state is excluded by name, and relocation is worse than costly here — §7's entire remaining breadth argument is a live-state fact ('22 version specs … 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none', which is what 'exercises both sides of the round-dependent skip reason' rests on), so a relocated copy either carries spec/.tp-review/ (reading the live state, which S1's first clause forbids) or resets every spec to round 1 and loses the only shape §7 claims the corpus buys. The result is that the one property §7 designates as blocking the release is the one property no suite obeying §6.1 can run.
suggestion: Decide which of the two S1 protects and say so. Either (a) exempt property 8 from S1 and state the weaker condition it can actually meet — the gate may read the live state and must leave it byte-identical, naming the save/restore or read-only mechanism that achieves it — or (b) keep S1 absolute and redefine property 8's subject as a copied spec corpus, and then rewrite §7's breadth argument so it claims only what a copy preserves (section structure, size range) and drops the recorded-rounds claim it can no longer make.

finding: Property 3 asserts two incompatible things about the same byte string, so the two engineers who write it produce opposite assertions and one of them is guaranteed red. Sentence one: "strip the suffix property 1 fixes from an emitted body and the remainder contains neither clause string and ends with the newline §2.3 removes." Parenthetical/second clause: "the pre-clause body is the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes plus that newline." These cannot both hold. §2.3 constructs the emitted body as <original body, trailing newline removed> + 468-byte suffix, so emitted[:-468] is the original body with its newline already gone — it does NOT end with a newline, which is exactly why the parenthetical adds one back to reconstruct the pre-clause body. Engineer A writes assert.True(strings.HasSuffix(remainder, "\n")); engineer B writes assert.False(...). Property 3 is the release's only byte-level guard and it is not writable as stated.
suggestion: Delete "and ends with the newline §2.3 removes" from the first sentence and keep the parenthetical as the definition: the remainder is the pre-clause body minus its trailing newline, so the assertions are (a) len(emitted)-len(remainder) == 468, (b) remainder contains neither clause string, (c) remainder does not end with LF. State (c) explicitly if it is meant to be checked, since it is the only observable trace that the strip happened.

finding: Property 5's exit-0 branch is unsatisfiable for a case its own definition of "recognised" admits, so the test cannot be written. §4.2.1 defines the exit-2 set as a name "absent from the corpus for either phase, from skipped_roles, and from the built-ins"; everything else exits 0 "with prompts: [] and that role's reason echoed from skipped_roles." Run against this repository's own 4+4 corpus, `tp audit spec/0.36.0.md --role tester` names a role present in the corpus for the review phase — therefore recognised, therefore not exit 2 — while an audit invocation's skipped_roles contains no `tester` entry, so there is no reason to echo. The property demands an echo of something that does not exist. This is a different hole from the known one about the one-prompt modes: it needs no `--perspective` or `--verify`, it fires on the plain default invocation of `tp audit`, and the name that triggers it is one this repository's own corpus ships. Two engineers split: one asserts exit 0 with an empty reason, one asserts exit 2 for a cross-phase name.
suggestion: Either narrow "recognised" to the corpus *for the phase the command runs* (so a cross-phase name exits 2 with the existing hint), or add a third outcome for "recognised, not emitted, no skipped_roles entry" and pin what the payload carries in place of the reason. Whichever is chosen, say explicitly whether a mode that computes no skipped_roles (--verify, --perspective) can reach the exit-0 branch at all.

finding: Property 3 cannot be implemented as written, because tp's own changed-section embedding puts the clause strings inside the pre-clause body. Property 3: 'strip the suffix property 1 fixes from an emitted body and the remainder contains neither clause string'. §2.3 states the mechanism that defeats it in its own words — 'tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim into the prompt' — and §2.2/§3.2 hold the two clauses in fenced code blocks inside sections of this spec. Measured on the shipped binary: a two-round fixture whose §2 contains the §2.2 clause in a ```text block, edited between rounds, emits all four prompts (implementer, tester, architect, regression) with the clause string present verbatim in the body, outside any appended suffix. §1.1 calls property 3 'the only guard that runs' after two prose guards were abandoned, so the release's one arithmetic guard fails on the very spec that defines the clauses, in every round where §2.2 or §3.2 is a changed section — which is most rounds of this cycle. An implementer has no stated escape: property 3 is an unconditional 'contains neither'.
suggestion: Restate property 3 as a suffix-only claim that does not quantify over the remainder's content: 'the emitted body ends with exactly the 468-byte suffix, and the body minus its last 468 bytes plus one LF equals the body the emitter assembles before the append'. Both sides are then produced by the same emission and the clause may legitimately occur earlier in the text. If a 'no second occurrence' claim is wanted at all, scope it to the region after the prompt's last section heading, and say explicitly that occurrences inside embedded spec text do not count.

finding: Property 5's exit-0 branch has no source to read in four of the five modes §4.2.2 legalises the flag in, because those payloads emit no skipped_roles key at all. Property 5: a recognised-but-not-emitted name 'exits 0 with prompts: [] and that role's reason echoed from skipped_roles'. Measured on the shipped binary: `tp review <spec> --perspective documentation --docs-path X` emits keys [spec, perspective, docs_path, docs_structure, prompts, review_loop]; `--perspective testing --test-path X` and `--perspective regression` emit no skipped_roles either; `--verify --findings f` emits [spec, spec_ref, spec_path, prompts, review_loop]. Only the default mode carries the key. So for `tp review <spec> --verify --findings f --role architect` — architect is in this repo's review corpus, hence 'recognised' by §4.2.1's test and therefore not the exit-2 case — the implementer must invent all three of: whether to synthesise a skipped_roles key that mode has never emitted, which reason string to put in it (tp computes none, and none of §4.2.1's five reasons describes 'this mode does not use the corpus'), and whether adding the key breaks property 4's 'every other top-level key is unchanged'. §4.2.1's five-reason table is presented as exhaustive and does not contain this case.
suggestion: Add a sixth outcome to §4.2.1 covering a name that is recognised but is not a member of the invocation's match set for a reason tp does not tabulate — which is every corpus name in a --perspective or --verify invocation. State its exit code, whether skipped_roles appears, and the reason token (a new one such as `not-in-this-mode` is cheaper than reusing an existing one). Then reword property 5 so its echo clause applies only where skipped_roles is emitted, and say what property 4 permits when a key is added.

finding: §1.1 makes two claims about §6.2 property 3 and this round's rewrite of §6.2 falsified both, in the exact direction §1.1 exists to prevent. §1.1 opens: "**467 bytes per role prompt.** The arithmetic is written out because §6.2 property 3 fixes it as an exact integer, and an earlier draft stated 468 — one more than its own construction in §2.3 produces", and closes: "this table is the derivation, and §6.2 property 3 fixes the net delta as an integer, which is the only guard that runs." Property 3 now opens "The 468 bytes are the whole change" and its own parenthetical concedes the swap: "467 is the net delta of §1.1's table; 468 is the suffix." So property 3 fixes the suffix, not the net delta; the reason §1.1 gives for writing the table out names a property that does not state 467; and "the only guard that runs" now pins 468 — the very figure §1.1 identifies as the earlier draft's error. Checked over §6 as a whole: no property anywhere asserts 467.
suggestion: Fix the two §1.1 references rather than the table: say that §6.2 property 1 fixes the construction and property 3 fixes the 468-byte suffix, and that 467 follows from them by derivation — or add the net delta to property 3 as a second pinned integer so §1.1's sentence becomes true again.

finding: §1.1 twice names §6.2 property 3 as the running guard for 467, and property 3 as rewritten this round fixes 468 and explicitly declines to assert 467. §1.1 line 32: "467 bytes per role prompt. The arithmetic is written out because §6.2 property 3 fixes it as an exact integer." §1.1 line 53: "§6.2 property 3 fixes the net delta as an integer, which is the only guard that runs." Property 3 opens "The 468 bytes are the whole change" and closes "(467 is the net delta of §1.1's table; 468 is the suffix. The arithmetic is derivation, not a second measurement.)" — i.e. it asserts the suffix length and states that the net delta is derived rather than measured. So after this round no property in §6 asserts 467 at all, and §1.1's claim that a guard runs on it is false. This matters to a test writer specifically: §1.1 says the guard is "the only" thing standing between the two figures and a third drift, and a test written from §1.1 (len(after)-len(before) == 467) needs a pre-clause emission the spec has withdrawn every mechanism for (§6.3 rows 1–2), while a test written from property 3 (len(suffix) == 468) is buildable but is not the assertion §1.1 promises.
suggestion: Rewrite §1.1's two cross-references to say what property 3 actually fixes — the 468-byte suffix, from a single emission — and drop the claim that the net delta is guarded, or state plainly that 467 is derived from the table and nothing asserts it. The table already carries the derivation; one accurate sentence replaces two false ones.

finding: "A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty" is stated as the sentence that saves the exit-0 rule — "so no hook change is needed, only the instruction" — but the spec never says where the instruction is carried, and in the exact case it governs there is no carrier. The only channel this release adds to a unit is prompt text (§2.2, §3.2), and by construction the exit-0 case emits `prompts: []`, so no prompt exists to hold the instruction. No property in §6.2 covers it either: properties 1–3 are conditioned on an emitted prompt, property 5 fixes only the exit code, the empty prompts[] and the echoed reason. So a QA engineer cannot write a pass/fail test for the one behaviour that keeps stop-role-incomplete.sh from refusing the unit, and two implementers ship different things — one adds a top-level notice/hint key to the empty payload, one adds nothing and assumes the agent knows.
suggestion: Name the carrier and give it a property: either the exit-0 payload carries a fixed instruction string on a named top-level key (pin the key and the string, as §2.2 pins its clause), or the sentence is moved out of §4.2.1 into the agent definitions/brief and §4.2.1 says so — but then say which path is left uncovered, since the interactive path loads no definition (§2.1).

finding: §4.2.1 requires 'A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty' and identifies the hook that punishes the omission, but the release provides no channel that carries the instruction to that unit. Everything §2 and §3 add is appended to a prompt body, and this is precisely the case where prompts is []; the only remaining agent-readable text is review_loop.instruction, which §6.2.3 property 12 requires to be *stripped* of orchestrator-addressed directives under --role and which §4.2.3 says is assembled 'across nine assignment sites' with no single place to add a sentence. The unit's brief is `tp review <spec> --role <id>`, so a unit whose role is dropped no-checklist-items runs that command, receives an exit-0 payload with an empty prompts array and no instruction addressed to it, and there is nothing in the emission that tells it to touch $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-<id>.ndjson.part at all. The requirement is therefore stated in the spec and enforced by hooks/stop-role-incomplete.sh but delivered to nobody, which is a hang-adjacent wasted round-trip that §4.2.1 itself says the sentence exists to prevent.
suggestion: Name the surface. Either add a key to the exit-0-with-empty-prompts payload (for example an `instruction` or `note` string saying to write an empty findings file and exit), or state that the sentence belongs in agents/tp-reviewer.md and agents/tp-auditor.md and make editing those definitions part of this release's scope — §2.4 already argues the definitions are the right home for a standing rule under tp run, and this is one. If neither is in scope, drop the requirement and say the empty-prompt unit's first stop refusal is accepted.

finding: S1's second half is not assertable by any test, so half of the condition this round added cannot pass or fail. "spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ are byte-identical after the suite runs **and** unchanged throughout it." The first half is a before/after hash comparison — deterministic and cheap. The second is a statement about every instant *during* the suite's own execution, and a Go test suite has no vantage point from which to observe it: the only processes that could mutate those directories are the suite's own invocations, so the suite would have to watch itself. Two engineers diverge completely — one adds an fsnotify/polling watcher goroutine (racy, and its own failures are timing-dependent), one re-reads the same before/after hashes and calls the second half satisfied by the first, which is exactly the reading S1's own text says is insufficient.
suggestion: Restate the second half as a property of the invocations rather than of time: every `tp review`/`tp audit` invocation the suite makes runs against a tree whose review state it does not share with the repository — then the assertion is that the live paths are untouched (hash before/after) and that each invocation's state directory is the isolated one. If the intent is genuinely that no intermediate state exists, say which observable stands in for it (e.g. each invocation's own reported round number is constant across the suite), because that is what a test can actually compare.

finding: Property 12 states a different rule from the §4.2.3 blockquote it implements, and the added half is unsatisfiable. §4.2.3 fixes the rule as "Under `--role`, no sentence of `review_loop.instruction` may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support", and explicitly rejects the deletion framing: "The rule is a property, not a list of sentences to delete." Property 12 requires the `--role` form to be "a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one" — deletion only, replacement forbidden — and swaps the criterion from payload-support to "orchestrator-addressed directives". Measured on this spec's round-11 emission, `review_loop.instruction` is six sentences and five of them direct panel-only actions (spawn a sub-agent for each prompt; merge/verify/resolve then `--record`; repeat until `--status --check` exits 0; process the regression prompt first "before or together with the three role prompts"; run an uncounted `--perspective regression` delta pass). The sixth, "Read the spec at <path> before processing each prompt", is itself panel-plural. So the strict subset property 12 mandates leaves the key empty, or leaves one sentence that still fails §4.2.3's own criterion — and property 12 forbids the one repair that would make it honest, a unit-addressed replacement sentence. No section sanctions an empty `review_loop.instruction`, and property 4 licenses the key to change, not to vanish.
suggestion: Drop "is a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one" and restate property 12 as §4.2.3's blockquote, then add what the `--role` form must still carry (which spec to read, where to write) so the key cannot legally reduce to the empty string.

finding: Property 12's second sentence — "Without `--role` it is unchanged." — names no baseline, and the only two candidates give a tautology and an unbuildable test respectively. Reading A: unchanged from what the same binary emits without --role. That compares an unrestricted invocation with itself; the test passes by construction and can never fail, so it buys nothing. Reading B: unchanged from the predecessor binary's emission — which is the very comparison property 9 was withdrawn this round for being unobtainable ("no test in one binary can obtain the predecessor's emission", §6.3 row 1). So property 12 re-introduces, in one unqualified clause, the baseline the section next to it just retired. Property 4 avoids this by naming its comparand explicitly ("the otherwise identical invocation without the flag"); property 12 does not.
suggestion: Either delete the sentence (property 4 already fixes the no---role payload against the unrestricted one) or give it property 4's form and say what it is compared against, and if the intended comparand is the predecessor release, mark it withdrawn in §6.3 alongside property 9 rather than leaving it as an assertion.

finding: Property 3 contradicts itself across one sentence pair, and §2.3 settles which half is wrong. It asserts: "strip the suffix property 1 fixes from an emitted body and the remainder contains neither clause string and ends with the newline §2.3 removes." §2.3's construction removes that newline *before* the suffix is appended, so the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes ends with whatever preceded the removed newline — never with a newline. Property 3's own next clause concedes exactly this: "the pre-clause body is the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes **plus that newline**" — the newline has to be added back precisely because the remainder does not carry it. An implementer who writes the first assertion literally gets a test that fails on every correct build by one byte, which is the failure round 6 recorded against §6.1's earlier blockquote, now inverted: that draft omitted the strip, this one asserts the stripped byte is still there.
suggestion: Delete "and ends with the newline §2.3 removes" from property 3's first sentence. The reconstruction clause already states how the pre-clause body is recovered, and the only assertion the remainder can carry about its last byte is that it is *not* the newline §2.3 strips.

finding: Property 3's negative half — "the remainder contains neither clause string" — is exactly the class of assertion §2.3 records as measured-and-defeated on this spec, reintroduced twelve lines from the section that fixed it. §2.3: "tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim into the prompt, and this document contains the string `## Unit framing`, so on the round-3 architect prompt the heading occurs **three** times. Any anchor drawn from the prompt's own prose can be forged by the spec under review." §2.2 (line 104) and §3.2 (line 240) carry both clause strings verbatim in fenced blocks. Any round that edits either section — the most likely repair this release will make, since the clauses are its only normative text — puts the clause literal into the changed-sections block of every role prompt, and the pre-clause remainder then contains a clause string with the suffix intact and correct. Property 8 makes the release gate iterate every spec in the repository, this one included, so the forgery is inside the gate's own subject set rather than hypothetical.
suggestion: State property 3 positionally rather than by presence — the remainder does not *end with* either clause, and the emitted body contains the suffix exactly once at its end — or scope the presence-negative to a spec that does not quote the clauses and say so, since §2.3 already proved presence assertions over prompt prose are forgeable here.

finding: Property 4's rule quantifies over top-level keys and its exception names a sub-key, which leaves review_loop's other members unconstrained and produces two incompatible tests. "Every other top-level key is unchanged **except `review_loop.instruction`** ... `review_loop` is a top-level key." Engineer A reads the exception at the granularity of the rule and excludes the whole `review_loop` object from the comparison — under which convergence, round, converged, stale, previous_findings, required_clean_rounds and consecutive_clean may all differ under --role and the test still passes. Engineer B compares `review_loop`'s members individually, exempting only `instruction` — a strictly stronger test that fails an implementation A accepts. §4.2.3 states the intent ("It does not claim the convergence statement... `convergence` is a *sibling key* of `instruction`"), but §4.2.3 is rationale and property 4 is the assertion, and property 4 as written does not carry it.
suggestion: State property 4's comparison at one granularity: "the payload with --role is byte-identical to the unrestricted payload except that prompts[] holds one entry and review_loop.instruction changes per property 12; every other key at every depth, including review_loop's remaining members, is unchanged." That is one assertion both engineers write the same way.

finding: Property 6 classifies by 'mode', but emptiness is a property of the invocation, and two modes §4.2.2 puts in the legal column emit nothing until a companion flag is supplied — so the implementer cannot tell which branch to write. Property 6: '--role is accepted in every mode that emits prompts and refused with exit 2 in every mode that emits none.' Measured: `tp review <spec> --verify` without --findings exits 2 ('--verify requires --findings'), and `--perspective testing` without --test-path exits 2 ('--test-path is required when --perspective=testing'). Both invocations emit no prompts, so a per-invocation reading of property 6 requires --role to be refused there — contradicting §4.2.2's table, which lists --verify and --perspective as legal. Worse, §4.2.2 fixes the order: 'The refusal is evaluated before the mode's own argument validation, so the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict rather than a missing --findings.' Under the per-invocation reading that ordering rule produces exactly the wrong hint — it would tell an operator that --role is illegal with --verify, which the same section says it is not. The per-mode reading avoids that but leaves property 6's own words ('every mode that emits none') matching invocations the table calls legal, so neither reading can be implemented from the text alone.
suggestion: Say that the legal/refused classification is a static property of the mode flag, fixed by §4.2.2's table and not recomputed per invocation, and that in a legal mode the mode's own argument validation runs normally and its error wins. Then reword property 6 to quantify over §4.2.2's table rather than over 'modes that emit prompts', and confine §4.2.2's before-validation ordering rule to the refused column, where it is the only thing it was ever meant to cover.

finding: The exit-2 hint is required to have content and its content is never pinned, so the only deterministic assertion available is on the exit code. §4.2.1: "exits **2**, with a hint listing what the invocation would have emitted." Property 5: "exits **2**, with a hint naming what the invocation would have emitted." Neither "listing" nor "naming" fixes a shape, a channel or a separator, and the two verbs are not obviously the same requirement. A QA engineer has four readings with different tests: the hint contains every emitted role's name; it contains at least one; it names the roles as a comma-joined list; nothing is asserted beyond exit 2. §4.2.1 leans on the hint carrying real information ("the exit-2 case has exactly one hint because it has exactly one cause"), so an assertion that only checks the exit code lets a hint that says nothing useful pass — which is the failure mode §4.2.1's own paragraph exists to prevent.
suggestion: Pin the hint the way §2.2 pins its clause: give the exact template with the substitution point (e.g. "unknown role %q; this invocation emits: %s" over the emitted roles in payload order), and add a property asserting the emitted role names appear in it. If the wording is deliberately left to the task's acceptance, say so and state the one thing the property does assert — that every role the unrestricted invocation would emit is named.

finding: §4.2.1's recognition test spans both phases while its exit-0 payload is single-phase, so a role name from the other phase's corpus is recognised and unserviceable. The exit-2 rule fires only for 'a name tp recognises nowhere — absent from the corpus for either phase, from skipped_roles, and from the built-ins'. In this repository the corpus is 4 reviewers plus 4 auditors, so `tp audit <spec> --role tester` and `tp review <spec> --role go-safety` both name a role that is present in the corpus for one phase — recognised, hence not exit 2 — and that will never appear in the other phase's skipped_roles, because engine.roleUnits and the emitter both resolve the active corpus per phase. The exit-0 branch then has no reason to echo, exactly as in the --perspective case, and this is the more likely operator mistake of the two: with §4.2.3 making --role a unit's own first command, a copy-pasted brief across phases produces it directly, and the operator gets a silent exit 0 with an empty panel where a hint naming the phase would have ended it.
suggestion: Make the recognition test phase-scoped: 'a name absent from the corpus for *this* command's phase, from skipped_roles, and from the built-ins exits 2'. Then add one sentence to the hint rule saying that a name belonging to the other phase's corpus is named as such, since that is a distinct and cheap message and §4.2.1's 'one cause, one hint' argument does not survive the cross-phase case.

finding: S2's closing sentence — "Those four inputs are pinned by the test." — refers to an artifact §6 no longer contains and gives the implementer nothing to write. §6's own preamble records that the nineteen numbered tests were removed ("This section states properties, not tests"), so "the test" has no referent: there is no singular test, and no property in §6.2 mentions the round number, the loop budget, the consecutive-clean count or output_path. Separately, S2's normative half ("No fixture encodes this repository's review state") is a constraint on how the suite is written, not a claim any test can evaluate — no assertion can observe that a fixture does not exist. So of S2's two halves, one is unassertable by nature and the other points at nothing. Two engineers: one pins the four values in every property test as an explicit fixture, one pins them once in a shared helper, one skips them because no property demands them.
suggestion: Attach the four inputs to the properties that need them (7, 8 and 11 are the ones whose comparisons the round number and skipped_roles move) and state them as a precondition of those properties, e.g. "properties 7 and 8 hold the round number, loop budget, consecutive-clean count and output_path fixed across the invocations they compare." Then drop "pinned by the test", and keep the no-stored-blob half as the stated rationale it is.

finding: This round re-adopts, for §6's properties, the exact document-about-the-document mechanism §1.1 retired two rounds ago for drifting — and pays a withdrawn list slot to protect it. §1.1 records that two anti-drift devices "were documents about the document, and both drifted faster than the thing they guarded", and concludes "There is no third attempt". §6.2 then installs one: twelve bare ordinals, split this round across three new subsections (§6.2.1/6.2.2/6.2.3), addressed by number from outside — measured on the file, 10 numeric citations from five sections (§1.1 lines 32 and 53; §2.3 lines 151, 162, 166; §4.2.3 line 401; §4.4 line 463; §7 line 607 twice and line 618) plus 4 more inside §6.2/§6.3. The cost is already visible in the same text: property 9 is retained purely as an empty slot — five lines of normative-list real estate that assert nothing — because renumbering would break those ten citations, while §6.3 exists precisely to hold withdrawn constructions so "the properties stay readable". This spec has already spent rounds on stale numeric cross-references into §6 (round 9's stale-cross-ref-after-table-repair), and every reviewer, every round, must resolve an ordinal against a list that has now been reorganised twice. A number is the one identifier that carries no information about what it names, so it cannot be checked by reading and drifts silently.
suggestion: Give each property a short kebab-case name and cite it by name plus subsection — "§6.2.2, concatenation-equals-payload" rather than "§6.2 property 7" — so a citation is self-checking, the list can be reordered without a sweep, and a withdrawn item can be deleted into §6.3 instead of parked. That removes property 9's five lines outright and makes the ten external citations verifiable by grep rather than by counting.

finding: §6.3 is introduced with an explicit organising rule for §6 — "Four constructions were specified and withdrawn. They are listed here rather than beside the properties they used to encumber, so that the properties stay readable and the reasons stay found" — and property 9 breaks it in the section §6.3 was created to clear. Property 9 is a five-line withdrawal narrative left inline in the numbered property list, and its subject is §6.3's own first row: property 9's "a claim about this release versus its predecessor… no test in one binary can obtain the predecessor's emission" is row 1's "A cross-version baseline (`v0.35.2`'s emitter) | A `go test` binary compiles one tree; the old emitter is not callable from the new one". The same dead end is now recorded twice, with two differently worded reasons that can drift apart, and the property list carries a hole an implementer must read past to reach property 10.
suggestion: Reduce property 9 to a one-line placeholder that preserves the numbering and points at its reason — "9. *Withdrawn* — see §6.3, row 1." — leaving the reason stated once, in the table built for it.

finding: The release gate multiplies its own cost 38x for two distinct cases, and §7's justification is measured on a dimension property 7 does not compare. Property 8 promotes property 7 to "every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for"; §7 defends that in three paragraphs, the last of which argues breadth buys "section structures no fixture author would think to write". But property 7's subject is the concatenation of prompts[] against the unrestricted payload's prompts[] — a comparison over panel MEMBERSHIP and ORDER, not over prompt content. Measured just now on this tree with the current binary, TP_* cleared, over all 39 spec/*.md (38 emit; spec/0.28.0.md exits 4): the panel has exactly TWO distinct values across the whole corpus — ('architect','ax-economist','implementer','tester') 27 times, and the same four plus 'regression' 11 times. So 38 unrestricted emissions plus ~163 per-role emissions, per command, per test run, buy two cases of the property being asserted; a two-spec fixture buys the same two. §7 already concedes the skips are not bought ("The other four skip reasons do not occur here and must be built as fixtures"), which leaves shapes — and shapes are what property 7 holds fixed. The cost is not CPU (the 38 unrestricted emissions took 0.6 s): it is the isolation apparatus S1 exists to build. Measured: that same read-only sweep left 37 untracked files and directories under spec/.tp-review/ plus one modified snapshot — precisely the side effect S1 forbids, and the reason §6.1 must relocate the spec and stand up a git-history working tree. The release's largest unbuilt construction is charged to a breadth that yields one extra case.
suggestion: State what property 7 actually varies and size the gate to it. Either (a) keep property 8 but justify it as a cheap regression sweep over an already-isolated harness rather than as coverage, and delete §7's "section structures" sentence, which describes prompt content the property never compares; or (b) scope the gate to the distinct panel values (one spec where regression emits, one where it does not, both commands) and say in §7 that the remaining 36 emissions re-run those two cases. Either way add one line to §1.1 pricing the isolation harness beside the 467 bytes, since it is now the dominant cost of the release and the only reason the gate is not free.

finding: §1.1's fourth anti-drift mechanism in four rounds is false in the round that wrote it: the guard it names does not assert the figure it headlines. §1.1 makes two claims about property 3 — line 32, "The arithmetic is written out because §6.2 property 3 fixes it as an exact integer", where "it" is the 467-byte net delta; and line 53, "§6.2 property 3 fixes the net delta as an integer, which is the only guard that runs" — and §2.3 line 151 adds a third, "That is 4 separator bytes, which is the figure §1.1 prices and §6.2 property 3 fixes." Read as rewritten this round, property 3 asserts none of them. Its assertion is over 468: "The 468 bytes are the whole change… the pre-clause body is the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes plus that newline." 467 appears only in a parenthetical gloss with no predicate attached ("467 is the net delta of §1.1's table; 468 is the suffix"), and 4 appears nowhere in §6.2 at all. So the headline figure of the release's cost section is asserted by no property, and the sentence that closes three rounds of drift-fighting ("There is no third attempt: this table is the derivation") rests on a guard that guards the other constant. The document carries two integers where the mechanism determines one, and the one a reader is asked to trust is the unguarded one.
suggestion: Two words, in one of two places. Either rewrite property 3's opening as "the net delta is 467 and the appended suffix is 468", asserting both, so §1.1's and §2.3's three claims become true; or drop the claims — say in §1.1 that property 1 fixes the construction and the net delta follows from it, which is accurate, and delete "which is the only guard that runs" and §2.3's "and §6.2 property 3 fixes". The second is the cheaper fix, since property 1 plus the two byte-fixed clause strings already entail 467 and no separate integer needs guarding.
